query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, loss of toughness at intermediate temperatures is governed by rapid nanosegregation of the principal elements (e.g., Cr, Mn, and Ni) to grain boundaries, which locally reduces cohesion and triggers intergranular brittle fracture rather than the conventional precipitate‐induced embrittlement observed in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20) with minimal preexisting secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled intermediate-temperature exposure (e.g., tensile deformation or annealing around 500–700°C) under conditions that mimic service loading rates.
generation.conditions: Intermediate temperatures (500–700°C) at strain rates typical of service conditions; experiments should be compared against room-temperature mechanical behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale clusters enriched in Cr, Mn, and Ni along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures without long aging times, thermal activation promotes a rapid, short-range diffusion of the principal elements to the grain boundaries. This nanosegregation diminishes grain-boundary cohesion, thereby localizing stress and triggering brittle, intergranular crack initiation under mechanical loads—contrasting with the transgranular ductile behavior observed at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under intermediate-temperature tensile testing, samples that display evidence of nanosegregation at GBs will show reduced ductility and a transition to intergranular fracture. Conversely, HEAs engineered with preexisting Cr-rich precipitates that act as sinks for these embrittling elements should exhibit improved ductility and more uniform fracture behavior.
generation.baseline: The same single-phase HEA testing at room temperature exhibits ductile, transgranular fracture with high toughness and no significant grain-boundary embrittlement.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to be most pronounced in tests at intermediate temperatures (500–700°C) and at moderate strain rates. At very high temperatures (where other diffusion or phase separation phenomena dominate) or very low temperatures (where segregation kinetics are suppressed), the mechanism may not be active.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics and extent of nanosegregation, and the influence of minor impurity levels, require further quantification. Variability in the alloy composition can also affect the segregation behavior, which introduces uncertainty in the predicted embrittlement threshold.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of microstructurally similar single-phase HEA samples. One set is left in the as-cast/homogenized condition while the other is pre-treated to promote the formation of Cr-rich secondary precipitates at grain boundaries (designed to 'absorb' the mobile embrittling elements). Perform tensile tests at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 650°C) and in parallel conduct atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM analyses to detect and quantify grain-boundary segregation. Compare fracture modes and ductility between the two sets.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, percentage elongation)
Fracture surface analysis (SEM/TEM) to distinguish intergranular versus transgranular fracture features
Grain-boundary composition analysis via atom probe tomography or EDS in TEM
Quantification of nanosegregation extent at GBs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If (a) both the as-cast and pre-treated samples show similar mechanical performance and fracture modes with no significant grain-boundary nanosegregation differences, or (b) ductility loss at intermediate temperatures is observed without detectable nanosegregation at grain boundaries, then the hypothesis is refuted.
